stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-48, an act to amend the Crop Insurance Act, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, with interruptions like that there really will be no opportunity to continue the discussion on Bill C-48.
I should like to comment on the remarks of the Deputy Prime Minister during the course of this debate because he certainly left a number of questions open, in my view. He accepted an amendment last week. As I recall the incidents of last Thursday afternoon, he only accepted one small amendment. With respect to the other one, he was sort of asleep at the switch and the amendment got through without him noting it.
I was disappointed that he did not accept the amendment with regard to the establishment of an advisory committee because the difficulties that we have with climate change in this country are very severe. We have seen literally thousands of farmers in southern Ontario especially, as well as in the three prairie provinces, lose

March 19, 1990
Government Orders
their farms over the last three or four years because of climatic change. It does not seem to be improving very much. Thus Bill C-48 is a very important bill.
The minister tried to make the argument this afternoon that this matter was widely discussed. It clearly was widely discussed last July by a very large group of farmers from right across the country. They all agreed that the funding should be one-third, one-third, and one-third; it being shared by the federal and provincial governments as well as by the farmers. When the governments of the provinces and the federal government got together in Prince Albert at the end of July last year, there were no farmers there. A deal was struck which essentially cut up the cash in such a way that the federal government is paying 25 per cent, the provinces are paying 25 per cent, and the farmer ends up continuing to pay 50 per cent.
Although we agree with most of the amendments to the crop insurance legislation, this change really negatives the whole bill. Farmer group after farmer group- practically every group that came before us-said that the problem with it was that although the coverage was moving up from 70 per cent or 80 per cent to 90 per cent, the farmers could not afford to pay it.
That is why they were all opposed to it in the national meeting they had in early July. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture, which represents the largest and most broadly based farm group, said in its presentation before the legislative committee about the 25, 25, and 50 formula: "While in some provinces this formula results in a relatively equal tripartite cost sharing of total program costs, in others the producers may end up paying up to 77 per cent more than the federal or provincial governments in their contributions. Uniformity and fairness across the country is essential to a national crop insurance program".
That is why the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and all constituent groups across the country are opposed to this measure. In its final summation before the committee it stated: "As a final note, we would like to point out that in order to increase producer confidence and therefore participation in the program an improved and enhanced program must offer an affordable price. Our members are skeptical of the likelihood of the continuation of an affordable program as it appears that
the federal share of crop insurance is being systematically reduced".
I think that is really the problem with the whole of the government's Green Paper. The paper the minister tabled in the House and about which he spends a lot of time talking essentially provides for two main proposals. One is that the government will reduce support programs to agriculture, which is what it has been doing for the last year. Every program that the government is involved in is being cut in one way or another. The only thing that it followed through on was the drought assistance that it promised in the 1988 general election. Last year the budget was cut by some $500 million to agriculture. Crop insurance alone was cut by some $200 million over two years. There is a whole list of other things including advance payments and other programs which were cut.
If we look at the spending estimates which were tabled a month or so ago, we see that drought assistance has been cut by $365.6 million. We see that the two-price wheat system has been cut by $56 million. We see that $42 million in statutory payments on crop insurance has been reduced. Yet there is all this talk about there being improved coverage. There is going to be improved coverage all right, if one can afford it.
If we look at the cost of the program to various groups we see that it is not going to be affordable. Several members from my caucus including the member for Lambton-Middlesex, the member for Prince Edward- Hastings, the member for Kent-Essex and the member for Essex-Windsor met last Friday with a number of wheat, com and soybean producers. Most of these groups, which included com producers, soybean producers, fruit and vegetable producers and winter wheat producers were all arguing that the cost of the coverage is simply too high.
For instance, for winter wheat producers, we see the cost of the coverage going from 4.4 per cent to 7.2 per cent. That is just to go from 80 per cent coverage to 90 per cent coverage. That is a 63 per cent increase to move up only 10 per cent in improved coverage.
Likewise, with corn, it is 64 per cent. For soybeans it is a 50 per cent increase. Similarly, for producers of red spring wheat in Saskatchewan, the cost of coverage goes
March 19, 1990

from 12.6 per cent for 70 per cent coverage, to 19.5 per cent for 90 per cent coverage. We are looking at an almost 50 per cent increase in the cost of the coverage. This type of increase is similar for almost all crops.
Although the bill provides for improved coverage, nobody is going to take it. That is exactly the problem we are facing today. Producers, whether they are com producers, soybean producers or wheat producers in southwestern Ontario, or wheat, barley and other crop producers in the west, are demanding a special financial aid program. They do not have any of the tools that the American producer has. The American wheat grower today has a target price of about $4 U.S. that he is guaranteed. He has a loan rate of something around $2. He has a deficiency payment between those two figures.
About two weeks ago a couple of members from each caucus in the House met with a group from the Agriculture Leadership Training Program of Ontario. There were some 30 young agriculturalists or farmers who met with members of Parliament and put the argument to us that we hear every place we go in this country. It is that there is no certainty.
The government has taken away the advance payments program, which was roughly the same as the American loan program, although not quite as good. There is no target price and there is no deficiency payment. Nobody knows whether the whole special grains program, although very beneficial, is going to be there. It was triggered in 1986 in the middle of a provincial election in Saskatchewan. Will it be triggered this year? We do not know if there is going to be a provincial election. If we knew there was going to be a provincial election, then maybe it would be triggered, but maybe it will not be.
Tell us about the Liberals' special grains program.

I believe the hon. member for Crowfoot is talking about the Liberals' special grains program. Back in the late seventies and early eighties when wheat prices were at $5 or $6 a bushel, when we had a two-price wheat system and the cost of production was probably 50 per cent or 60 per cent lower than today, farmers did not need a special grains program because they were immensely better off than they are today.
We had the spectacle a week ago Monday night with the Premier of Saskatchewan, who is also the Minister of
Government Orders
Agriculture, pleading on province-wide television for financial support from the federal government. He had already met with the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds and the Deputy Prime Minister. He has probably discussed it with the Prime Minister, yet he has to go on province-wide television to plead for support. The Minister of Agriculture had this all laid out for him by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool last October and November, which was asking for a special injection of $500 million to put the crop in the ground this spring.
Ontario com and soybean producers have made the same arguments. They are facing the same difficulties, as I told the members of our caucus last week. Yet it goes on month after month: December, January, February, March, April. Farmers just do not believe that there is going to be any special grains program or that there is going to be an interim payment under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. It is just left up in the air. What is going to happen? Nobody knows.
Compounding that problem is the situation we have with the banks. I was in Saskatchewan a week before last meeting with members of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool from around the Yorkton area. It was the same thing with grain producers in southwestern Ontario last week. The banks are essentially closing down Canadian agriculture. They will no longer lend money on the basis of the equity the farmer has in the land itself. The only basis on which they will lend money is on a cash flow basis. As I have already said the price of many grains-wheat, soybeans and com-is below the level where they will have cash flow. We are caught in this bind.
The minister met with the Canadian Bankers' Association last Thursday night. He tried to reassure us today. It seems to me that the whole thing is so hollow. He is talking about all the stakeholders, all the players in the game-the provincial government, the Farm Credit Corporation, the banks, the lending institutions in this country and the federal government.
How can anybody else in the game take the minister seriously when he is sitting there with the producers demanding financial support since last November and no financial support is forthcoming? Will there be a special grains program? Will there be an interim payment on ASA? Nobody knows, and there we sit.

March 19, 1990
Government Orders
There is great, great uncertainty. The minister's comments today leave everybody wondering what is going to happen in this situation. Clearly this legislation just provides for more and more ad hoc programs because farmers will not use it.
There is another special concern for people from provinces like Prince Edward Island. It is not only the growers who are going to have extreme difficulty in meeting this new program. In provinces like Prince Edward Island they are going to have great difficulty with the provincial government coming up with their share of support.
I believe what is happening in Prince Edward Island is similarly happening in New Brunswick and perhaps in B.C. When we get to the end of the day we see that Ontario opposed it. With Quebec and Newfoundland, previously there really was not a great deal of support. For Prince Edward Island the costs are going from $150,000 a year to $650,000 a year. We are talking about $500,000 in additional costs to that small province with 130,000 residents.
How is the government of Prince Edward Island going to afford that? It is probably praying that the premiums will be so high that the farmers will not take out the insurance, because it does not know where it is going to get the $500,000 additional cost to its small province.
I do not have the figures for B.C. and New Brunswick, but I am sure that they have similar problems. The Deputy Prime Minister talks about this as though it was not a bill sprung on everybody in the middle of the night. It certainly was sprung on those four provinces that are opposed to it. It certainly was not what the farmers themselves asked for.
The angering part of this whole thing is that it is coming at a time when the United States is starting to work on a new farm bill which, we are told, will essentially be the same as the 1985 farm bill, and the United States is cutting its programs. That government is not reducing its deficiency payments or loan rates, but our government is reducing its support for crop insurance, for advance payments and for a whole series of programs, and we are doing it unilaterally.
That is simply not workable because we have to compete with those American producers. We do not
have an export enhancement program, although the premier of Saskatchewan is calling for that and it is probably a good idea if we are going to maintain our share of the world market. Our producers do not even have the programs that they had two years ago.
This bill will pass the way it is, regardless of how unworkable it is. The real issue today is whether the government is going to come forward with an emergency financial package. Every major farm organization has asked for it. The premier of Saskatchewan is asking for it and so far there is simply no response from the government even though seeding is only a month and a half away. I want to call attention to this. I do not know how it can be more firmly imprinted on the Deputy Prime Minister's mind and focused more dramatically to get action in this regard.
Clearly, the emergency need for funding is there, but we do need action on the farm debt problem. Last Saturday's Globe and Mail illustrates the type of problems that farmers in many parts of the country are facing. In that article, the premier of Saskatchewan pointed out:
"We're facing economic war in Saskatchewan," he said before meeting with the agricultural committee of the Canadian Bankers Association late Thursday. "Our farms are dying. It's a crisis."
He noted that 20,000 farmers-one-third the entire province-are faced with financial ruin unless they receive an immediate cash bailout of $500 million.
That is the $500 million that he went on province wide television a week ago last Tuesday to demand action on.
The article further states:
Moreover, he said, they need another $1 billion to tide them over until the harvest this fall and long-term help so they can carry a debt burden that has risen to more than $5 billion.
Imagine, Mr. Speaker, 60,000 farmers carrying a debt burden of $5 billion.
The urgency is for the government to act, yet it refuses to act. It is putting through a farm crop insurance program which is nickeling and diming and which is going to cause a great deal of problems because farmers will not take out enough coverage and we will have to continue on with this ad hoc program that is being demanded by the Saskatchewan farmers.
The uncertainty not only rests in grain and oilseeds, corn and soybeans, but in every sector of the Canadian agriculture economy today. If you talk to people who are in supply management, in poultry, in eggs and turkey
March 19, 1990

production, in the dairy industry, there is tremendous uncertainty. Last week, I asked the Minister for International Trade if he would give a commitment that in the proposal that they are putting before the multilateral trade negotiations in Geneva, Switzerland, this year, they would take the advice of the poultry producers and the dairy producers of the type of access that they would agree to under Article 11 negotiations of the GATT agreement. He gave me the usual non-answer answer. It is absolutely essential that we get a commitment from the government that it is not going to sell out the farmers.
In the free trade deal they did not take the advice. They appointed a special advisory group on international trade, SAGIT, represented by producers, processors and farmers. They made a recommendation that any commodity coming in from the United States, whether it was processed chicken or processed dairy products, that had more than 10 per cent by dry weight or volume of a supply management commodity, would be subject to import controls.
That recommendation of the SAGIT was never accepted. The government went ahead willy-nilly, signing an agreement where the tariffs came down from about 12 per cent to zero over 10 years and essentially gave away the whole supply management structure in that agreement. The Minister of Agriculture said: "Have no fears. We will put all those items from the tariff list over to the import control list and there will be no problems."
That was in January 1988. We knew that there were very serious problems because the chairman of the Senate trade committee in the United States, Mr. Lloyd Bentsen of Texas, immediately complained to Mr. Yeut-ter, the Secretary of Trade at that time, that this was breaking the agreement, that there was no provision in there, that they would take Canada to the GATT if they put those items on the import control list.
Sure enough, as soon as they put them on the import control list in December 1988, effective January 1, 1989, the United States petitioned GATT to establish a panel to see if putting those items on the import control list was a conflict of Canada's obligations under the GATT treaty. In September or October of last year the GATT came down with a decision stating that they were in
Government Orders
contravention and ultimately the government accepted it in early December.
There we were in the GATT negotiations with an incredibly weak hand to play, to say the least. It is hard to see how the government can play that hand, if one looks at the people who are opposed to Article 11 of the GATT. There is our free trade partner, the United States, the trading group that we are associated with, the Cairns Group, and now Professor Worley of the University of Guelph, who is an expert on the GATT negotiations, saying that he thinks the European Economic Community is going to oppose our position as well to strengthen and clarify Article 11 of the GATT.
Of course, there is also the off-hand comment to one of our officials by the United States Ambassador to GATT who stated: "Look, we don't really have to negotiate Article 11. All we have to do is get a couple more GATT panels on the other processed dairy products and we have total access to your market anyway."
While this may sound very complicated, it is very simple to the dairy producers of this country, those who have market-share quota, those who produce milk for the industrial production of processed dairy products, items like ice-cream and yogurt, cheese, skim milk powder and butter. With that border open into the United States, they can easily swamp our market and swamp those producers, many of whom are in the province of Quebec, if the GATT negotiations fail.
That is why I asked the Minister for International Trade the other day if the government would abide by the recommendation of the dairy farmers of Canada, which is to limit imports under the access to our processed dairy products to 5 per cent by value and 3 per cent by volume. That would leave the production of cheese, which has now about 9 per cent access and increase a number of other commodities which have no access now to 1 per cent. However, even 1 per cent is a lot of money. This is a $4 billion business, so 1 per cent is $40 million of access by the United States.
Mr. Speaker, you can understand why every dairy producer, every poultry producer, every egg producer in this country is extremely nervous about those negotiations. Our bargaining position was given away in the free trade deal. Our bargaining position at the GATT is extremely weak. We do not have many friends. Apparently we have the Swiss and the Austrians and some of

the Scandinavian countries with us, but compared to the power and influence of the European Economic Community, if Professor Worley is right, and compared to the United States that has vowed openly to do away with Article 11, and compared to the 11 or 12 countries in Cairns Group, our position is not strong.
That is not to say that we want to see the government not succeed in this, because doing away with the vibrancy, efficiency and viability of the poultry and dairy industry would be a disastrous blow. We would be facing the same kind of demands for financial support from that sector as we are facing in the grain, oilseed and com crops this year, if we were to lose out in those negotiations.
This bill makes some improvements. It looks good on paper, but the cost to producers is dramatically increased at a time when they cannot even borrow money on the equity they have in their farms. They can only borrow on the cash flow of their crops. Many farmers will not be able to afford the dramatically increased premiums which, in some cases, increased by 60 per cent and in some cases even more than that.
We want to see the government act immediately on the farm debt crisis and the farm financial crisis, because we are talking about the very future and the viability of our industry. We know it may be counter to the government's Green Paper, which is essentially to remove support programs and to make the industry wide open to world markets. We think that they should stop and look at survival of an industry which is facing horrendous difficulties in this coming year. It is an industry that is competitive. Our problem is coping with the international community, the massive subsidies in the United States and in the European Community. It is essential that we look at this from a global point of view. Are we going to have a viable agriculture industry which not only provides efficient food production in this country but provides a vibrant and effective rural community which is essential to the well-being of our country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on third reading debate of Bill C-48, an act to amend the crop insurance legislation. To give some background, I would like to spend a few minutes in the 20 minutes that
I have available to me to go through some of the international affairs that have affected the world of grain production and the impact that that has had on the farms of people on the prairies in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and northern British Columbia, and also as it affects grain production in central and Atlantic Canada. All grain producers producing crops in this country have been affected by the grain wars that have erupted between the two big power blocs, the European Economic Community and the United States of America.
Each war is quite unique. This particular one is centred on a question of who should be a producer of grains for exports in the world, with the Americans taking the position that they should be the pre-eminent exporters of grains and that other countries should be much smaller exporters of grains. In particular, the American viewpoint is that the Europeans really do not have any business exporting grain into world markets. That is an attitude that carries back to the last world wheat talks which failed, whereby the wheat exporters of the world were attempting to set a floor price beyond which countries that were participants in the wheat agreement would not offer grain.
The system of floor prices has been in effect for quite a long time; sometimes it worked and sometimes it did not. When wheat was in high supply, often some of the countries involved in the pact would begin to break the agreement.
From Canada's point of view, it was very often the United States which broke those agreements. It would find ways of offering some grades of grain and some types of grain below the floor price and that would eventually break the price. A number of times in my memory when Canada attempted to abide by the commitments under the International Wheat Agreement and held the price up, the consequence was that we sold very little grain in those periods of time because we were trying to abide by international rules.
I raise this because what we have been facing in rural Canada over the last decade almost, certainly in the last six or eight years, has been a heating up of the dispute as to who should be able to sell grain between the Europeans and the Americans. It got much warmer in 1985 with the introduction of the American farm bill which
March 19, 1990

had not only the plethora of subsidies that is endemic in the agricultural system of the United States of America, but an additional impetus to exports by including the Export Enhancement Program whereby the United States offers money to potential buyers of grain to buy their grain as opposed to somebody else's grain.
They began by offering incentives in the range of $7 per tonne. More recent sales this calendar year have gone over $20 per tonne. So the war is heating up.
I am a Canadian fanner, as are thousands of others in this country. We can understand the ups and downs of international marketing, and to some extent, even though there is a lot of politics in it, we have learned to accept and live with that. What we find very difficult to live with is when our own government refuses to come on side and be an advocate for us in those grain wars.
We can accept that there are times when other countries will be shooting at us and we will be caught in the crossfire, as we have been between the Europeans and the Americans. It is extremely difficult to accept our own government shooting at us as well. It is bad enough to duck the competition but when your own government starts shooting at you, you start to think that something is wrong. I submit that something is very wrong when, since re-election in 1988, the government has contributed to our misery in rural Canada by taking an additional $1 billion out of the pockets of farmers.
How have they done this? In the last two budgets, programs have been pulled away that had existed for a long time which were of benefit to rural Canada. For example, small programs such as the at and east freight rates encouraged western grain to go into Atlantic Canada, permitted workers in Atlantic Canada to load ships year round, and kept rail line workers busy ferrying grains from the Georgian Bay elevators over to Halifax and Saint John.
There was also a reduction of the crop insurance money that goes into crop insurance, the program we are debating here today. The Government of Canada has decided that it will not supply close to half of the premiums to cany the cost of crop insurance. After Bill C-48 that we are debating today is passed, instead of
Government Orders
farmers paying 50 per cent of the premiums and the federal government paying 50 per cent of the premiums, farmers will continue to pay at least 50 per cent of the premiums and the federal government will drop its contribution to 25 per cent and leave the provinces to pick up the other 25 per cent.
That will mean that farmers and rural people will be paying through their provincial taxpayers' pockets. For some of the larger provinces, this will not be too much of a problem. However, in provinces like Saskatchewan and Prince Edward Island where farmers and farming make up a great deal of the economy, taxes will increase quite perceptibly because the Gross National Product of those provinces depends very much on the production of field crops, whether they are potatoes, wheat, or some of the oilseed crops. It will make a big difference to the amount of taxes that provincial taxpayers will put into the crop insurance program.
That is where some of the controversy takes place. In the course of the building of the grain wars, the balance between the amount of money that a farm takes in and the amount that that farm has to spend on personal expenses and business reinvestment has changed remarkably. Up until about 10 or 15 years ago, approximately 50 to 70 per cent of a farm's gross income went out as expenses. In Saskatchewan, the crop insurance program covered 70 per cent of the average long-term yield for that province. If land was producing 30 bushels to the acre of wheat, the crop insurance program would cover 70 per cent of that, which would be something like 21 bushels per acre. This would virtually cover the actual cash outlays of those farms at that time.
Because of the grain wars and the downward pressure on price, most farms are now finding that even the most efficient with good crops have only about 10 to 15 per cent to spend on their own families and for reinvestment in the farm after all costs are paid.
The government's response at Prince Albert was to open up the crop insurance legislation so that the various contracts with the provinces between the federal government and the provinces could include crop insurance that would pay up to 90 per cent of the loss. The idea was to permit farmers to take out enough crop insurance to cover their cash losses if there was no crop.

Government Orders
I have no great objection to opening up the legislation to permit higher levels of coverage. I just point out that it is not going to address the income problem that is out there. Fiddling with crop insurance is not going to be the answer to a problem that is essentially a world price problem.
At one time, we had two sets of programs because we recognized that there were two problems that faced farmers. One was a production problem, for which we had crop insurance. It was not always as adequate as it could be, but the program is there and still will be there after C-48.
On the other hand, we had a price insurance program which went into place through two different sets of legislation. In the Wheat Board area of western Canada, the Western Grain Stabilization Act applied and we contributed 2 per cent of our sales to finance that. The federal government also contributed on a two for one basis. In the rest of Canada, price was protected under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. Farmers in those regions who had crops that were not of the six major grains in the Wheat Board region got coverage without paying premiums.
Anyone who has watched farming policy in the last number of years knows that one of the last acts of the old Liberal government and one of the first acts of the new Conservative government in 1984 was to make some fairly drastic amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act, with the idea of paying out a larger payment for a couple of years, on the assumption that the world price problems that were surfacing would go away.
Even when there is no political interference, world price problems generally have a cycle of about 15 years from the low through the high and back to the low. If I had any criticism of the Western Grain Stabilization program, it was that it had too short a vision. It looked at a 10 year period of time instead of the 15, which would have more properly reflected the reality of world price cycles.
After 1984, we shortened that up to seven years with the result that the program is now virtually useless. The fund is in deep deficit. No money is being paid out, and yet farmers needs are still there. That happened because the formula was changed to generate a quick, large pay-out around election time. It did its political job, but
it did not do its economic job of evening out farm incomes.
This particular legislation is permissive. As I said earlier, it fails to follow the government's own program of tripartitism, which involves provincial, federal and producer payments on an equal, one-third, one-third basis. Instead, the federal government has taken a quick-fix budget oriented approach to increase coverage which will increase premiums to producers, but the federal government will not increase the amount they pay on those premiums. In fact, it has decided instead to unload that responsibility onto the provinces.
While the federal government proposes to save $90 million in the year that is coming to a close and an additional $110 million in the fiscal year coming into play April 1, the provinces will have to pick that up. For the further coverage that may be possible with the opening up of the program to coverage up to 90 per cent, producers will have to pay extra premiums.
Just to give an idea of what that will mean, we got some figures from some of the witnesses from Ontario who appeared before us. They pointed out that for Ontario right now the average winter wheat producer pays $4.50 per acre for the basic coverage package. The new increased coverage will cost him an extra $1.79. That simply puts his coverage level 10 per cent higher than it was. He goes from an 80 per cent coverage to a 90 per cent coverage in the province of Ontario and that will cost that producer almost $1.80 per acre more.
Had this initiative been carried out on a tripartite basis, where the producer, the federal, and provincial governments paid equally, that extra coverage would have cost that Ontario producer of winter wheat an extra six cents per acre. We can see the dramatic difference that this makes in production costs to producers. For winter wheat, it is almost $1.80 an acre.
If we consider something like tomatoes, where the producer is now paying $41.50, enhancement to the program namely, going from 80 per cent coverage to 90 per cent coverage will cost him almost an extra $35 an acre. Under tripartite it would have cost him an extra $20. So the tripartite system is one that producers had expected and were looking forward to as being part of
March 19, 1990

the package, and there is some disappointment that that was not the case.
As well, one of the confusing things at committee level was dealing with 10 different contracts. The federal government has a different system of contracting crop insurance with each of the provinces. The rules affecting a producer of commodities like wheat or peas in one province are sometimes quite substantially different from the rules that affect a producer of the same commodity in another province.
For instance, the federal government makes ad hoc changes to the contracts that it puts on. Sometimes these are encouraged by the producers in the area, but they are never fair. For instance, at the end of last week there was an announcement about the final multi-year disaster benefit for 1989 to those regions of prairie Canada that had a further continuation of the drought. For some regions it was the third consecutive year of drought.
It would be possible to treat them on a farm-by-farm basis in the province of Saskatchewan because of the kind of crop insurance records and program that we have. We have had crop insurance since either 1960 or 1961, which took over from the old Prairie Farm Assistance Act. The region of the province where I live, which is reasonably well watered most of the time, was the pilot area to start that insurance program. We paid our 1 per cent, not to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act but into crop insurance premiums. Some of us did not have very many losses during that period of time, but it meant that if we did have a loss on our farm, we would get paid for the losses that we had, rather than having to depend on all of the surrounding townships having losses before we qualified.
The government has forgotten those lessons of the PFAA and has reintroduced the multi-year disaster benefit. Even though your farm had a drought for three years in a row and you collected the maximum crop insurance, you did not qualify for the extra 10 per cent coverage benefit unless you were in a municipality that bordered on three other municipalities which make up a district of four municipalities suffering the same disastrous occurrence. If you happen to live in a municipality that is isolated then you are just out of luck. Many people found that they were out of luck and were not able to get any assistance, as a result.
Government Orders
We believe that this particular bill is not entirely beneficial for Canadian farmers. We think it is simply an excuse for the federal government to unload some of its spending responsibility for farmers on to the provinces, and an excuse to charge farmers more for crop insurance. As I said at the beginning of my speech, that is consistent with its move to take more than a billion dollars of extra funds out of farmers' pockets in the last year and a half since its re-election. If the federal government would simply recompense those funds it has already taken out of farmers' pockets unjustly, farming would be in much better shape than it is today.

Mr. Speaker, the last federal budget indicates that the amount to be spent on crop insurance for 1989-90 would be reduced by $90 million and a further $110 million decline was projected for 1990-91 fiscal year. How will this affect the likely returns for farmers who are collecting crop insurance in the next year? Can it be projected into the pocketbooks of the farmers during the next year?

Mr. Speaker, the $91 billion from last year and the $110 million of savings to the federal Treasury in the coming fiscal year are to be brought about as a result of unloading part of the cost on to the provinces.
If the provinces sign new contracts increasing the amount of coverage to the farmer, permitting contracts which would allow the farmer to increase his coverage from the existing 70 per cent in Saskatchewan up to 80 per cent which was available in the past crop year, and as high as 90 per cent in the province of Ontario, which was,

Government Orders
available last crop year, the federal government is projecting that it will mean higher premiums being paid by the fanners. Between them the federal government and the provincial governments have to match those premiums.
Since the federal government is proposing to save some $90 million last year and $110 million in the coming fiscal year, that means the provincial governments will have to pick up the same amount that the federal government saves. The provinces will be having to raise approximately an extra $100 million as a result of this initiative by the federal government.
Farmers will be paying slightly higher fees if they opt for the higher coverage levels which I think they will be forced to do given the change in the production economics at the farm level whereby close to 90 per cent of the gross sales of a farm go out directly for cash costs.
If the farmer wants to stay in business after having a crop loss he will need crop insurance that will cover at least 90 per cent of his cost. Therefore, premiums will rise at the farm level, and coverage will be up. The main problem for provincial governments will be that they will have to raise quite a bit more money to make up the deficit of the $90 million last year and $110 million this year.
Mr. Speaker, will the vegetable growers, fruit growers and non-grain growers be affected in the same way?

Mr. Speaker, we did not get to see all the contracts which exist, but my understanding is that increased coverage will be available to vegetable and fruit growers as well.
The premiums will be somewhat higher. I believe I mentioned tomato growers in southern Ontario having to pay an extra $35 per acre for premiums for that extra 10 per cent coverage. It is a fairly high rate, but given the kind of cost-price squeeze that is affecting farmers now, some of them may be forced by their creditors and their lending institutions to take the higher coverage levels,
just for the mutual protection of the farmer and the banker.

Mr. Speaker, I feel privileged to have the opportunity to speak to Bill C-48. As I was listening to some of my colleagues speak to this issue, I started to reflect on what has caused this lack of pride that we, as Canadians, seem to have in our agricultural community.
I want to go back to an experience I had in 1986.1 was flying to Cuba with our former Minister of Agriculture, the Hon. Eugene Whelan. The Liberals were not in power then and Mr. Whelan was long gone as a minister. I remember, as he was walking to the back of the plane, everyone gave him a friendly greeting, saying that it was nice to have him back. We went on to Cuba where we received a very warm welcome from officials.
One evening I asked the Cuban officials why they had such respect for this man who had been away for so long. One of them said that when they were in need the minister made sure that they had Holstein cattle to help feed the people and when they had fever break out from time to time, Canadian veterinarians would go to Cuba. There seemed to be a sense around the world that Canadian agriculture had a place of pride.
About two months ago, I was in Moscow to speak on an environmental issue. I was amazed by the lineups for food that I saw every morning on my way to the conference. There were lineups of 200 people or 300 people at every food store in the city. These people were afraid that if they did not get to the food stores early in the morning they would not have lunch or dinner. The food that was in these stores made me feel ashamed.
When I returned home I was struck by the fact that I do not think we really give the farmers of this country enough respect or enough time. We have seen a government that has been retreating from its national responsibility over the last five or six years. I am afraid that situation has now reached the farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
You are always away. You don't know what is going on here.
March 19, 1990

The hon. member says that we do not know what is going on here. If the hon. member watched IT-5 last night, he would know that 50 per cent of that show was dedicated to the farmers of Canada, who are crying out desperately for government, at all levels, to give them some time and attention. Even though I am an urban member, many of my constituents are phoning my office and telling me that we are not giving enough time to the agricultural community of this country.
I admit readily that many constituents do not understand what crop insurance is. I understand that the government is trying to redefine and reshape its priorities and put more responsibility in the provincial hands. At the same time I do not think the government is realizing that agriculture is not a business. It is like a vocation. I suggest, in my humble opinion, that the government does not realize completely the sacrifices of farmers and the the desperate financial shape the farmers of this country are in. If it did I think that we would be spending a lot more time on this issue.
Very few people in this House realize that I have been in agriculture for over 22 years. I do not grow crops but I have been involved and have had an operational farm for over 22 years. Even though I am not involved in it day to day I hear the stories from my own farm manager and our neighbours about how desperate the situation is.
The desperation seems to stem from two or three areas. First, many of our farmers are of an age where they would like to take life a little easier. They see that everyone else in the country has a certain quality of life and that as they get a little older they seem to be able to take things a little easier.
However, in the agriculture community this is not the case. Many of the farmers who are most active in this country today are in their early sixties and some are in their late sixties. This is a tremendous strain for them.
We see that their sons and daughters not wanting to stay on the farms. They are tempted because of the quality of life not to stay in rural Canada but to go to the urban centres. Who is going to carry on these family farms? From coast to coast we are seeing a complete deterioration of the family farm.
Government Orders
I know that members opposite are not designing this kind of a situation. I cannot imagine any man or woman who would want to see that kind of thing happen. The problem is that there does not seem to be an aggressive approach to promoting and enhancing the family farm. There does not seem to be enough awareness in the urban communities of the importance of the family farm and the health of the family farm. There does not seem to be enough communication to the people at large.
He has a hobby farm.

There does not seem to be enough communication that family farms are vital to our economy. It is vital in terms of our experts. The hon. member for Simcoe North talks about me trying to give a lecture about family farms-
From Broadview-Greenwood.

He knows about many farms in his own community where they are having a very difficult time now, where sons and daughters of those farmers in his own riding are leaving those farms. They are so close to the metropolitan areas that there is a disincentive factor.
Welcome to the 20th century.

Welcome to the 20th century he says. That is the attitude we get when we are trying to talk constructively about the family farm in this House. That is precisely the problem. This government is so pre-occupied with the retreat from national governments, so pre-occupied with cutting things like-

Where? VIA Rail, unemployment insurance, farm programs coast to coast. Cutting back on crop insurance responsibility and adding it on to the provinces. Right now you have disadvantaged provinces-

speechtext: They all agree. The farmers agree. You don't know what you are talking about.

There is the smugness and the arrogance of the members opposite when we are trying to make people aware of a group in our society right now wich is crying out.

We are trying to show that we on this side of the House care about the agricultural community in this country. Never before have the farmers been in such desperate straits. There are farm foreclosures day after day. Lines of credit are being cut back.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext: What have you done for the long-term dairy policy?

It is an incredible thing for someone who initially, when he came to this House, seemed to show a sense of respect for a community he came from. Now, all of a sudden, those members seem to have all the answers. They do not have all the answers and that is why the agricultural community of this country is in such desperate shape.
The Conservatives are not listening any more. They do not want to listen. They just want their own design, which is a massive decentralization of the national government. The only way we are going to put the agricultural community of this country back in shape is if this Chamber takes some leadership and we start putting some pride and a sense of appreciation back into the agricultural community.
I realize this is a complex issue, and that we must address the debt and deficit. The greatest resource we have in this country is our agricultural community. We in the city as we walk along the Danforth see in restaurant after restaurant plates piled high with food and every grocery store filled with every product one could conceivably imagine. We live in a cocoon in the urban areas of this country.
We are taking our agricultural community for granted. It is time we gave agriculture a higher priority and made sure that we develop policies in this country that will give our farming community a greater sense of respect and appreciation. We have to show them that we in this Chamber really care about their direction and their future. We have to get our youth back on the family farm. We have to make sure that those people out there right now, who are facing increasing difficulty in acquiring new machinery and equipment, know that we care.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to ask the hon. member where in the world
would he ever get the notion, and why would he ever say it, even if he read it in a comic book or otherwise, that farming is not a business?

Mr. Speaker, did the hon. member say that I said that farming is not a business? I correct myself. I am well aware that agriculture is a business.
My comment was that it is more than a business. It is a vocation, a part of our cultural heritage, and it is a way of life. That is the point I was trying to make.

I would like to ask the hon. member to justify how he can say that the government today does not care about farming, when the support for farming has increased 650 per cent from the time the Liberal Party was governing this country.
How can he claim that the Liberals cared more when they did not have drought assistance, a special grain program or the $51 billions that went for support of the farm industry? How can he come to the House of Commons and make the claim that they are somehow more caring for the farming industry, when there is nothing in the public accounts of Canada that would give any documentation whatsoever that that might even be slightly factual?

Mr. Speaker, this government has an incredible way of playing gymnastics with figures and percentages. The hon. member says 650 per cent. I do not know whether he is including the sum of money toward drought assistance. I do not know exactly what he means.
I do know one thing. Ask the agricultural community of this country if it has the same sense of pride in its work, in its state, in the general fabric of this country today, compared to 1984 and before. I can tell you that a great number of farmers are not satisfied. They are not happy. They think a lot more can be done.
